title: The Solar System
description: Explore our cosmic neighbourhood planet by planet.
author: Bilge

units.title: The Sun and Its Neighbours
units.description: Meet our star, the rocky planets and the Moon.

exercises.title: The Sun is a star
exercises.body: The Sun is the **star** at the centre of the Solar System. It holds about **99.8%** of all the mass in the system. The planets stay in orbit thanks to the Sun’s gravity.
exercises.example: If the Sun were a basketball, the Earth would be about the size of a peppercorn.

exercises.question: What kind of object is the Sun?
exercises.explanation: The Sun is a star: it makes its own light and heat. Planets do not produce light.

exercises.statement: Almost all of the mass in the Solar System is in the Sun.
exercises.explanation: Yes: about 99.8%. All the planets, moons and asteroids share the tiny remainder.

exercises.title: An 8-minute delay
exercises.body: Sunlight takes about **8 minutes** to reach the Earth. So the Sun you see in the sky is really the Sun as it was 8 minutes ago.

exercises.text: Sunlight reaches the Earth in about {{8}} minutes.
exercises.explanation: Light is very fast, but the Sun is very far: it crosses about 150 million km in 8 minutes.

exercises.question: What keeps the planets in their orbits around the Sun?
distractors: The light the Sun gives off
exercises.explanation: The Sun is so massive that its pull holds every planet in place.

exercises.question: Which of these are true of the Sun?
answers: It is at the centre of the system
exercises.explanation: The Sun sits at the centre and produces light. It is the Earth that orbits, and the Sun is made of hot gas.

exercises.question: What is the name of the star at the centre of the Solar System?
exercises.explanation: That is where the system gets its name: the Solar System.

exercises.front: How long does sunlight take to reach the Earth?

exercises.title: Four rocky neighbours
exercises.body:
The four planets closest to the Sun are the **rocky planets**. From nearest to farthest:
1. Mercury
2. Venus
3. Earth
4. Mars
Each has a solid surface you could stand on. Mars is called the **Red Planet** because of its colour.

exercises.question: Which planet is closest to the Sun?
exercises.explanation: The order is Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars.

exercises.question: Put the rocky planets in order, from closest to the Sun to farthest.
exercises.explanation: Earth is third; our next neighbour outward is Mars.

exercises.title: The hottest-planet surprise
exercises.body: The hottest planet is not Mercury, the closest one, but **Venus**. Its thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat inside; this is called the **greenhouse effect**. Its surface is about 465 °C.
exercises.example: Like a car left in the sun with the windows shut: heat gets in but cannot get out.

exercises.statement: The planet closest to the Sun is also the hottest planet.
exercises.explanation: The hottest planet is Venus. Mercury is closer, but it has no thick atmosphere to hold the heat.

exercises.question: Match each planet to its feature.
exercises.explanation: Now you know all four rocky planets.

exercises.text: Venus’s thick atmosphere traps heat; this is called the {{greenhouse effect}}.
exercises.explanation: The greenhouse effect is the atmosphere holding heat like a blanket.

exercises.question: Build the correct sentence.
exercises.explanation: Mars gets its colour from iron oxide, that is rust, on its surface.

exercises.question: Which planet is third in order from the Sun?
exercises.explanation: Mercury, Venus, Earth: our home is third.

exercises.title: Our only moon
exercises.body: The Moon is the Earth’s only natural satellite. It goes once around the Earth in about **27 days**. The Moon makes no light of its own; it **reflects** light from the Sun.

exercises.statement: The Moon makes its own light, just like the Sun.
exercises.explanation: The Moon is like a mirror: the brightness we see is reflected sunlight.

exercises.question: About how long does the Moon take to go once around the Earth?
exercises.explanation: About 27 days. That is also where the word “month” comes from.

exercises.title: Why do we have seasons?
exercises.body: The Earth spins on its axis once a **day** and goes around the Sun once a **year**. The seasons are caused not by distance from the Sun but by the Earth’s **axial tilt** (about 23.5°): through the year, different hemispheres receive the Sun’s rays more directly.

exercises.question: What is the main cause of the seasons?
distractors: The Earth moving closer to and farther from the Sun
The Sun’s heat changing through the year
exercises.explanation: If it were distance, both hemispheres would have summer at once. Instead, one has summer while the other has winter.

exercises.question: Match each length of time to the motion.
pairs: One spin of the Earth on its axis
One trip of the Moon around the Earth
One trip of the Earth around the Sun
exercises.explanation: Day, month and year: all three units of our calendar come from a turn in the sky.

exercises.text: The Earth’s axial tilt is about {{23.5}} degrees.
exercises.explanation: With a tilt of 0 there would be no seasons; 23.5 degrees gives us four.

exercises.question: Order these motions from the shortest time to the longest.
items: One spin of the Earth on its axis
One trip of the Moon around the Earth
One trip of the Earth around the Sun
exercises.explanation: 1 day, about 27 days, 1 year.

exercises.question: Which of these are true of the Moon?
answers: It is the Earth’s natural satellite
exercises.explanation: The Moon is a satellite, and it only reflects.

exercises.question: The Moon goes once around the Earth in about 27 days. About how many days do three trips take?
exercises.explanation: Three trips is roughly three months; the word “month” comes from “Moon”.
exercises.hint: Multiply the time for one trip by the number of trips.
exercises.solution:
1. One trip: 27 days
2. Three trips: $27 \cdot 3 = 81$ days

units.title: Giant Planets and Beyond
units.description: Gas giants, ice giants and the story of Pluto.

exercises.title: Jupiter and Saturn
exercises.body: After Mars come the **gas giants**: Jupiter and Saturn. They are made mostly of hydrogen and helium and have no solid surface to stand on. **Jupiter** is the largest planet in the Solar System.

exercises.question: Which is the largest planet in the Solar System?
exercises.explanation: Jupiter is so big that more than a thousand Earths would fit inside it.

exercises.statement: Jupiter has a solid surface you could walk on.
exercises.explanation: Gas giants have no ground to land on; the gas just gets denser the deeper you go.

exercises.title: A giant storm and rings
exercises.body: Jupiter’s **Great Red Spot** is a giant storm that has raged for centuries and is bigger than the Earth. **Saturn** is known for its magnificent **rings**, made of pieces of ice and rock.

exercises.question: Match them up.
pairs: What gas giants are made of
exercises.explanation: That completes the gas giants’ ID card.

exercises.text: Saturn’s rings are made of pieces of {{ice}} and rock.
exercises.explanation: The rings are not one solid piece: they are countless bits of ice and rock, from dust grains to house-sized chunks.

exercises.question: Rocky planet or gas giant?
exercises.explanation: The four inner planets are rocky; Jupiter and Saturn are gas giants.

exercises.question: Which planet is famous for its rings?
exercises.explanation: Other planets have thin rings too, but none are as spectacular as Saturn’s.

exercises.front: What is the Great Red Spot?
exercises.back: A giant **storm** on Jupiter that has lasted for centuries and is bigger than the Earth.

exercises.title: Uranus and Neptune
exercises.body: The two outermost planets are the **ice giants**: Uranus and Neptune. Uranus spins almost **on its side**. **Neptune** is the planet farthest from the Sun.

exercises.question: Which planet is farthest from the Sun?
exercises.explanation: The order ends like this: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune.

exercises.statement: Uranus spins almost on its side.
exercises.explanation: Its axis is tilted so far that it moves along its orbit like a rolling ball.

exercises.title: What happened to Pluto?
exercises.body: In 2006 Pluto was reclassified as a **dwarf planet**. That left **8 planets** in the Solar System. Beyond Neptune lies the **Kuiper Belt**, full of icy bodies like Pluto.

exercises.text: There are {{8}} planets in the Solar System; Pluto counts as a {{dwarf planet}}.
exercises.explanation: Since the 2006 decision the number of planets has been 8.

exercises.question: Put the outer planets in order, from closest to the Sun to farthest.
exercises.explanation: First the two gas giants, then the two ice giants.

exercises.question: Build the correct sentence.
exercises.explanation: The farthest planet is Neptune; the closest is Mercury.

exercises.question: Which group does each belong to?
exercises.explanation: The four outer planets split into two pairs; Pluto is in a class of its own.

exercises.question: What is the region beyond Neptune, full of icy bodies, called?
exercises.explanation: Pluto is a member of this belt too.

exercises.title: Between Mars and Jupiter
exercises.body: Millions of rocky pieces orbit between the paths of Mars and Jupiter: this is the **Asteroid Belt**. Its largest object is **Ceres**, big enough to count as a dwarf planet.

exercises.question: Between which two planets is the Asteroid Belt?
exercises.explanation: The belt separates the rocky planets from the gas giants.

exercises.statement: Asteroids are made mostly of gas.
exercises.explanation: Asteroids are made of rock and metal.

exercises.question: What is the largest object in the Asteroid Belt?
exercises.explanation: Ceres is both the largest in the belt and a dwarf planet.

exercises.question: Dwarf planet or planet?
exercises.explanation: Ceres and Pluto are dwarf planets.

exercises.title: Icy travellers
exercises.body: **Comets** are made of ice and dust. Near the Sun their ice turns to vapour and forms a bright tail, which always points **away from the Sun**. Small pieces that burn up in our atmosphere are **shooting stars**; a piece that reaches the ground is a **meteorite**.

exercises.text: A comet’s tail always points {{away from}} the Sun.
exercises.explanation: Particles streaming from the Sun push the tail outward.

exercises.question: What are comets mostly made of?
exercises.explanation: That is why they are also called “dirty snowballs”.

exercises.question: Match them up.
pairs: A piece burning in the atmosphere
A piece that reaches the ground
A traveller of ice and dust
exercises.explanation: All three are small bodies of the Solar System.
They are small bits of rock and dust burning in the atmosphere.

units.title: Moons
units.description: The remarkable moons of other planets.

exercises.title: Galileo’s four moons
exercises.body: Jupiter has four large moons: **Io**, **Europa**, **Ganymede** and **Callisto**. Ganymede is the **largest moon** in the Solar System. Io is famous for its volcanoes, Europa for the ocean beneath its icy crust.

exercises.question: Which is the largest moon in the Solar System?
exercises.explanation: Ganymede is even bigger than the planet Mercury.

exercises.question: Match each moon to its feature.
exercises.explanation: All three orbit Jupiter.

exercises.statement: Europa is thought to have an ocean beneath its icy crust.
exercises.explanation: That makes it one of the most intriguing places in the search for life.

exercises.question: Which of these are moons of Jupiter?
exercises.explanation: The Moon belongs to the Earth, and Ceres is a dwarf planet.

lessons.title: Titan and the Moons of Mars

exercises.title: A moon with an atmosphere
exercises.body: **Titan** is Saturn’s largest moon and the only moon with a **thick atmosphere**. Mars has two small moons: **Phobos** and **Deimos**.

exercises.question: Which moon has a thick atmosphere?
exercises.explanation: Titan’s atmosphere is even denser than the Earth’s.
Phobos and Deimos.

exercises.question: Which planet does each moon belong to?
exercises.explanation: Two of Jupiter’s big four, Saturn’s giant and the two little ones of Mars.

exercises.front: What sets Titan apart from other moons?

units.title: Secrets of the Sun
units.description: Why the Sun shines, and what its spots and wind are.

exercises.title: A giant fusion furnace
exercises.body: In the Sun’s core, **hydrogen** atoms join to form **helium**; this is called **fusion**. The energy released reaches us as light and heat. The core is about **15 million °C**, the surface about 5,500 °C.

exercises.question: What process produces the Sun’s energy?
exercises.explanation: The Sun does not burn like a fire; atoms fuse together.

exercises.question: Build the correct sentence.
exercises.explanation: Hydrogen is the fuel of fusion; helium is the product.

exercises.statement: The Sun’s core is cooler than its surface.
exercises.explanation: The core is millions of degrees; the surface is thousands.

exercises.question: Order from coldest to hottest.
exercises.explanation: About 15 °C, 465 °C, 5,500 °C and 15 million °C.

exercises.title: Spots and wind
exercises.body: **Sunspots** are regions that look dark because they are cooler than their surroundings. The Sun also streams charged particles into space: the **solar wind**. Near the Earth’s poles these particles create the **auroras**.

exercises.question: Why do sunspots look dark?
exercises.answer: They are cooler than their surroundings
distractors: They are holes in the surface
exercises.explanation: A cooler region gives off less light.

exercises.text: The auroras are caused by the {{solar wind}}.
exercises.explanation: The sky glows when charged particles hit the atmosphere.

exercises.statement: The solar wind is charged particles streaming out from the Sun.
exercises.explanation: This wind also pushes comet tails outward.

exercises.question: What are the colourful lights seen in the sky near the poles called?
exercises.explanation: In the north they are also called the northern lights.

units.title: Moon Phases and Eclipses
units.description: Why the Moon changes shape and how eclipses happen.

exercises.title: The Moon doesn’t change shape
exercises.body: Half of the Moon is always lit; how much of that lit half we see decides how it looks. The phases in order: **new moon**, **first quarter**, **full moon**, **last quarter**. One cycle takes about **29.5 days**.

exercises.question: Order the phases, starting from the new moon.
exercises.explanation: Then it returns to new moon.

exercises.question: In which phase does the Moon look fully lit?
exercises.explanation: At full moon we see the whole lit face.

exercises.statement: The phases happen because the Moon really shrinks and grows.
exercises.explanation: What changes is how much of the lit half we can see.

exercises.text: One cycle of the Moon’s phases takes about {{29.5}} days.
exercises.explanation: This is where the calendar month comes from.

exercises.title: A game of shadows
exercises.body: In a **solar eclipse** the Moon passes between the Sun and the Earth and covers the Sun. In a **lunar eclipse** the Earth is in between and its shadow falls on the Moon.

exercises.question: What passes in between during a solar eclipse?
exercises.explanation: The Moon moves between the Sun and the Earth.

exercises.question: Match each eclipse to its explanation.
pairs: The Earth’s shadow falls on the Moon
exercises.explanation: In both, the three bodies line up.

exercises.statement: In a lunar eclipse the Earth is between the Sun and the Moon.
exercises.explanation: That is why a lunar eclipse only happens at full moon.

exercises.question: Build the correct sentence.
exercises.explanation: The Moon does the covering; the Sun is covered.

units.title: The Journey of Discovery
units.description: From telescopes to spacecraft: how we came to know the Solar System.

exercises.title: Galileo looks up
exercises.body: In 1610 **Galileo** turned his telescope to the sky and saw four moons circling Jupiter. It was strong evidence that not everything orbits the Earth.

exercises.question: Who first observed Jupiter’s four large moons?
exercises.explanation: That is why they are called the Galilean moons.
The telescope had only just been invented.

exercises.statement: Galileo’s observations supported the idea that everything orbits the Earth.
exercises.explanation: The opposite: they showed bodies orbiting another planet.

exercises.front: What did Galileo see around Jupiter in 1610?
exercises.back: Four large moons: **Io, Europa, Ganymede, Callisto**.

exercises.title: Human and robot explorers
exercises.body: In 1969 humans set foot on the Moon for the first time with **Apollo 11**. **Voyager 1**, launched in 1977, is the most distant human-made craft and has reached interstellar space. On Mars, robot rovers such as **Perseverance** roam the surface.

exercises.question: With which mission did humans first set foot on the Moon?
exercises.explanation: The year was 1969.

exercises.question: Match each craft to its achievement.
exercises.explanation: All three are milestones of exploration.

exercises.question: Order the events from oldest to newest.
What is the most distant human-made spacecraft?
exercises.explanation: It has been travelling since 1977.

units.title: Space by Numbers
units.description: Speed, distance, time, charts and a little space Turkish.

exercises.title: Distance, speed and time
exercises.body:
The distance covered at a steady speed is the speed multiplied by the time: $x = v \cdot t$

If you want the time, divide the distance by the speed:

$$t = \frac{x}{v}$$

**Light** travels about **300,000 km** every second; nothing in the universe is faster.
exercises.example: At 80 km per hour, in 2 hours you cover $80 \cdot 2 = 160$ km.

exercises.question: You know the distance and the speed. Which formula gives the time?
exercises.explanation: Distance = speed × time, so time is distance divided by speed.

exercises.question: Light travels 300,000 km per second. How many km does it cover in 2 seconds?
exercises.explanation: That is more than one and a half times the distance from the Earth to the Moon!
exercises.hint: In $x = v \cdot t$ the speed is 300,000 km/s and the time is 2 s.
exercises.solution:
1. Formula: $x = v \cdot t$
2. Put the values in: $x = 300{,}000 \cdot 2$
3. Result: **600,000 km**

exercises.statement: A vehicle going twice as fast covers the same distance in half the time.
exercises.explanation: In $t = \frac{x}{v}$, doubling the bottom number halves the result.

exercises.question: The Sun is about 150 million km from the Earth. How many seconds does light take to cover that distance?
exercises.explanation: So the sunlight you see right now set off about 8 minutes ago.
exercises.hint: Time = distance ÷ speed. Cancelling the zeros first makes it easier.
exercises.solution:
1. Formula: $t = \frac{x}{v}$
2. Put the values in: $t = \frac{150{,}000{,}000}{300{,}000}$
3. Cancel the zeros: $t = \frac{1500}{3} = 500$ s
4. Convert to minutes: $500 \div 60 \approx 8.3$ minutes

exercises.text: Light takes about {{8}} minutes to travel from the Sun to the Earth.
exercises.explanation: 500 seconds is a little more than 8 minutes.

exercises.question: Build the distance formula.
exercises.explanation: Distance is speed multiplied by time.

lessons.title: Mars Logbook
lessons.context:
**From the logbook of a Mars rover**

A day on Mars, called a *sol*, lasts about **24 hours 40 minutes**. A Mars year is **687 Earth days**. Gravity is about **38%** of the Earth’s. The rover covers **100 metres** per sol on average.

exercises.title: Read the passage first
exercises.body:
The next questions are based on the **logbook** of a Mars rover. The passage sits above every question; tap its header to close it and open it again.

If you get stuck, tap **Hint**; after answering, **See the solution** shows the worked steps.

exercises.question: According to the passage, what is a day on Mars called?
exercises.explanation: *Sol* is Latin for “sun”; it means one solar day on Mars.

exercises.statement: According to the passage, a Mars year is shorter than an Earth year.
exercises.explanation: 687 days is longer than 365: a Mars year lasts almost two Earth years.

exercises.question: How many metres does the rover cover in 30 sols?
exercises.explanation: Mars rovers are in no hurry: 3 km takes more than a month.
exercises.hint: Multiply the distance per sol by the number of sols.
exercises.solution:
1. In one sol: 100 m
2. In 30 sols: $100 \cdot 30 = 3000$ m
3. That is **3 km**

exercises.question: An athlete reads 50 kg on a scale on the Earth. What would the same scale read on Mars, in kg?
exercises.explanation: Your mass stays the same but your weight drops; on Mars you could jump much higher.
exercises.hint: To find 38% of a number, multiply it by 0.38.
exercises.solution:
1. Ratio: $38\% = \frac{38}{100} = 0.38$
2. Multiply: $50 \cdot 0.38 = 19$
3. The scale reads about **19 kg**.

exercises.text: A Mars year lasts {{687}} Earth days.
exercises.explanation: 365 days is the Earth’s year and 88 days is Mercury’s.

exercises.question: Match the facts from the passage.
exercises.explanation: You have read the whole logbook.

exercises.title: Bar chart
exercises.body: In a **bar chart**, the taller the bar, the bigger the value. Tap the chart to see a bar’s exact value; the button at the top right shows the same data as a table.

exercises.question: According to the chart, which is the smallest rocky planet?
exercises.explanation: The shortest bar is Mercury’s: its diameter is under 5 thousand km.

exercises.statement: According to the chart, Venus and the Earth are almost the same size.
exercises.explanation: The two bars are almost the same height; that is why Venus is called the Earth’s twin.

exercises.question: According to the chart, about how many **thousand** km is the diameter of Mars?
exercises.explanation: Mars is 6,779 km across: about half the Earth.
exercises.hint: Tap Mars’s bar, or see which grid lines its top lies between.

exercises.title: Line chart
exercises.body: A **line chart** shows how a value changes. Planets get colder the farther they are from the Sun, with one exception: **Venus**! Its thick atmosphere traps heat, making it hotter even than Mercury, which is closer to the Sun.

exercises.question: According to the chart, which planet is the hottest?
exercises.explanation: The line peaks at Venus: about 460 °C.

exercises.statement: According to the chart, the average temperature on Mars is below zero.
exercises.explanation: Mars’s point lies under the zero line: about −65 °C.

exercises.title: Function graph
exercises.body: For anything moving at a steady speed, the distance–time graph is a **straight line**. Light covers 300 thousand km every second: $x = 300 \cdot t$ (thousand km). Slide your finger along the graph to read the distance at any moment.

exercises.question: According to the graph, how many **thousand** km does light cover in 4 seconds?
exercises.explanation: $300 \cdot 4 = 1200$ thousand km, that is 1.2 million km.
exercises.solution:
1. Find $x = 4$ on the graph
2. The value on the line: **1200**
3. Check by calculating: $300 \cdot 4 = 1200$

exercises.question: According to the chart, which gas makes up most of the Earth’s atmosphere?
exercises.explanation: About 78% of the air we breathe is nitrogen; oxygen is only 21%.

exercises.title: Learn by listening
exercises.body: Bilge speaks Turkish too! In this lesson you learn the Turkish names of four objects in the sky **by listening**. The big button reads the word, the small one reads it slowly. If you can’t turn the sound on, skip the question with “I can’t listen now”.
exercises.example: Güneş = Sun · Ay = Moon · Dünya = Earth · Yıldız = Star

exercises.question: Match each word to its meaning.
exercises.explanation: Now you know four Turkish words.

exercises.question: What does the word you hear mean?
exercises.explanation: “Ay” means the Moon.

exercises.question: Type the word you hear.
exercises.explanation: “Güneş” means the Sun.

exercises.question: What does the sentence you hear mean?
exercises.explanation: *Dünya* is the Earth and *gezegen* means planet.
In Turkish, too, the planet’s name is capitalised: Dünya.

exercises.question: Type the word you hear.
exercises.explanation: “Yıldız” means star. The Sun is a star, too!
